A product page is server-rendered and appears quickly, but on a mid-range phone the "Add to cart" button responds late: the click is queued until the browser has downloaded and run the code for the review carousel, the specs table and the recommendations, none of which the user has scrolled to yet. The team's first fix is to wrap those sections in
. The bundle shrinks, but the server-rendered HTML now has gray skeletons where the reviews used to be, and the page can shift when the real content replaces them.

The belief: a server-rendered page is all or nothing. The browser has to download the page's JavaScript and hydrate the whole component tree before any of it responds, so the only way to send less code is to defer content, and deferred content means placeholders in the server's HTML.
Both halves describe real behavior. With full hydration, the app hydrates as one tree, and the hydration guide notes that event listeners aren't attached until hydration completes. And the
guide says that by default, when rendering on the server, defer blocks "always render their @placeholder" and their triggers aren't invoked. The belief simply stops at those defaults.
A hydrate trigger turns @defer into a hydration boundary
adds a second kind of trigger to

. According to the guide, a hydrate trigger tells Angular to "load that defer block's dependencies during server-side rendering and render the main template rather than the @placeholder". So the server's HTML contains the real reviews.

In the browser, the block's dependencies are still deferred, and its content "stays dehydrated until its hydrate trigger fires". Dehydrated means the user sees the server's HTML, but no component code for that block has been downloaded or run: no constructor, no listeners, nothing reactive. It's a picture of the reviews, which is all a user who hasn't scrolled down needs.
The trigger downloads, hydrates, then replays
When the trigger fires, the block fetches its dependencies and hydrates its content, reusing the server's DOM like any other
. If the user clicked inside the block before that,

has queued the event: the guide says events that match listeners in your components "are queued up and replayed once the hydration process is complete". Incremental hydration enables event replay automatically.
The trade-off is latency on that first interaction: a click on a dehydrated block waits for its chunk to download. That's fine for a "Show all reviews" button and wrong for the main call to action.

content.text: A block can list several hydrate triggers separated by semicolons, and Angular hydrates it as soon as any of them fires.
Hydrate triggers only cover the first load

Hydration only applies to server-rendered content, so hydrate triggers only apply to the initial page load. When a user reaches the same page through a client-side navigation, the regular trigger runs, and the
is rendered first. That's why the example keeps both kinds of trigger and the placeholders, and why the guide says you still need a
. Nested blocks hydrate from the top-most dehydrated parent down, and
on a block keeps its whole subtree static.

Until its trigger fires, nothing inside the block runs: no

, no effects, no listeners. A parent that queries a child component, or a service that expects it to register itself, finds nothing until hydration. The usual hydration rules still apply inside the block, too: the same DOM on both sides, and no direct DOM edits.
